objectives: Recognize and read common short-/e/ CVC word families.
Identify onset and rime in controlled word-family patterns.
Apply word-family knowledge without abandoning grapheme-by-grapheme decoding.
Read short-/e/ words in controlled connected text.
concepts: Words in a family share a rime.
Changing the onset creates a new word while preserving the rime.
Word-family recognition supports efficiency but must not replace decoding.

definitions.definition: A group of words sharing a common rime, such as -et or -en.
The initial consonant or consonant cluster before the vowel in a syllable.
The vowel and any following sounds in a syllable.

workedExamples: pet → p + et; change p to g → get.
hen → h + en; change h to p → pen.
bed and red share -ed while their onsets differ.
commonMistakes: Guessing a family word from context.
Using an untaught pattern in controlled text.

basic: Sort short-/e/ CVC words by family.
conceptual: Identify onset and rime in taught words.
application: Generate a new family word by changing the onset.
higherOrderThinking: Choose whether a word-family strategy still requires full grapheme checking.
mixedReview: Read short-/e/ families and previously taught vowel families while preserving decoding accuracy.

formulaOrFactBank: Word family = shared rime + changing onset
mistakeBasedRevision: If guessing occurs, return to grapheme-by-grapheme decoding.
weakTopicRevision: Practise the specific family causing confusion, then reread controlled text.

outcomes: Learner accurately reads taught short-/e/ word families.
Learner identifies shared rimes and changing onsets.
Learner uses family patterns as support while checking every grapheme.
Learner applies short-/e/ decoding in controlled connected reading.

questions.question: Which words belong to the -et family?
Which words belong to the -en family?
What stays the same in pet and get?
What changes when pet becomes get?
Which word can be made by changing the first sound in hen to /p/?
Which word belongs with bed and red?
Why should a learner still sound out a word in a word family?
options: To verify every grapheme and avoid guessing

questions.question: Which pair has the same rime?
Which word does NOT belong with pet, get, and wet?
If a learner reads pen as pin, what should they check?
Which word completes the controlled sentence: “The hen is ___.”
What is the safest strategy when reading a new -en word?
options: Decode the onset and rime, then check each grapheme

questions.question: Which set contains only short-/e/ CVC words?
Why use controlled text after word-family practice?
options: To apply accurate decoding in connected reading

questions.question: What is the main goal of this lesson?
options: Read short-/e/ word families accurately while maintaining full decoding and controlled reading
